Updated assessment incorporating SLOOS:

- Policy stance remains supportive: The FOMC maintained a near-zero funds rate and began a gradual taper, signaling confidence in the recovery while keeping conditions accommodative.
- SLOOS signals broadly easier credit supply: Banks eased standards across residential real estate (including jumbo, QM/non-QM, HELOCs) and CRE (multifamily, nonfarm nonresidential), and for consumer credit (credit cards, autos). Banks increased credit card limits and reduced auto loan rates. Foreign banks also eased CRE standards with stronger CRE demand; C&I standards/demand were mixed (domestic banks reported weaker contemporaneous C&I and auto demand but stronger expected demand for C&I and credit cards). Reasons cited include improved economic outlook, competition, stronger liquidity/capital positions, and higher risk tolerance.
- Cross-check with FSR: While the FSR highlights elevated asset valuations and nonbank vulnerabilities, the SLOOS indicates bank-intermediated credit is more available, which should support spending and investment and partially offset taper-related tightening risks.

Net: Credit conditions from banks are more supportive than previously assumed, nudging the outlook modestly more positive, though still tempered by elevated financial vulnerabilities.
